title: Can the skeleton crew sail?
allegory: Checking a circuit is like vetting a skeleton crew for a ship: it must sail as well as the full company when everyone else is replaced by stand-ins who only do the average job (faithful), sending the same people home from both must hurt both equally (complete), and every crew member must be needed in at least one situation (minimal).

chapters.name: A story that fits
chapters.note: but does it actually do the job?

cap.1: You have drawn a neat diagram of which parts of a model do a task. But a diagram that fits the pictures is a story, not a proof.
cap.2: After patching you have a candidate circuit, like IOI's 26 heads in 7 classes. You now need tests that it is the mechanism, not just a plausible story.
cap.3: Wang et al. proposed three explicit criteria, faithfulness, completeness and minimality, for what counts as having found a circuit rather than a story that fits the plots.

cap.1: Test it like a skeleton crew. Send everyone else ashore, leaving stand-ins who only ever do the average job. Can the crew still sail as well?
cap.2: Faithfulness: keep the circuit's heads live, replace every other head's output with its mean, and check the task metric (logit difference) nearly matches the full model's.
cap.3: Mean-ablate all components outside C, using means over a reference distribution, and require F(C) ≈ F(M), where F is the logit difference.

cap.1: Send the same sailors home from the skeleton crew and from the full ship. If the full ship copes much better, someone important was never on your crew.
cap.2: Completeness: knock out the same subset K from the circuit and from the full model, and the two scores should match. A gap means the model uses parts your circuit lacks.
cap.3: The incompleteness score |F(C∖K) − F(M∖K)| should be small for every K ⊆ C. Matching F(C) ≈ F(M) alone could hide missing parts whose effects cancel.

chapters.name: The hidden backups
chapters.verdict: Needed in some situation counts; needed in every situation is too strict.

cap.1: Some sailors only step up when the main one is gone. Test people one at a time and key sailors look optional, because a backup always covers.
cap.2: In IOI, backup name movers take over when the primary name movers are ablated. So single-head ablation systematically understates how much a head matters.
cap.3: Redundancy defeats one-at-a-time ablation, so minimality is existential: v is needed if removing it matters for some K ⊆ C∖{v}, for example once its backups are gone.

cap.1: For each sailor, find one situation where losing them really hurts. If there is none, they are a spare part and should be cut from the crew.
cap.2: Minimality: every head in the circuit must matter somewhere. Remove a set K first, then check that also removing v changes the score a lot. That gap is its minimality score.
cap.3: Minimality: for every v ∈ C there is some K ⊆ C∖{v} with large |F(C∖(K∪v)) − F(C∖K)|. [1.4.1] has you compute these minimality scores for the IOI heads.

cap.1: Three checks. Does the crew sail as well as the ship? Does removing the same people hurt both equally? Does every crew member matter somewhere?
cap.2: Faithful: F(C) ≈ F(M). Complete: F(C∖K) ≈ F(M∖K) for all K. Minimal: each v has some K where removing it changes the score a lot.
cap.3: Faithfulness tests sufficiency, completeness tests that no outside mechanism is used, minimality tests necessity under redundancy. All three use the same knockout metric F.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A diagram is a claim; these are the tests
Backups hide importance from single ablations
Only a verified circuit is safe to edit

cap.1: Before you trust an explanation of what a model is doing, or edit it, check the explanation is enough, complete, and has no spare parts.
cap.2: These tests turn 'my circuit' from a story into a claim you can check. If you plan to steer or ablate a mechanism, you need to know you found all of it.
cap.3: Faithfulness, completeness and minimality outlasted the IOI circuit itself: they are the standard for claiming a mechanism, and a prerequisite for trusting interventions built on one.

caption.1: Top row is your crew, bottom row sends people home. Send h1 home and h0 suddenly matters: h1 was its backup. Try adding spare h4, or dropping h3.
caption.2: Toggle C and K. Faithfulness compares circuit to model; completeness compares them after removing K; minimality shows each head's effect given K. Backups hide importance.

where_else: Any circuit you find later, whether built from heads, SAE features or transcoder latents
Minimal bug reproductions: enough to trigger the bug, nothing extra
Ablation studies in ML papers: remove a part and check whether the result survives
Engineering redundancy: a backup hides how much the primary matters until both fail

hamming.what: Three tests of a proposed circuit: it does the task alone (faithful), nothing important lies outside it (complete), and every part matters somewhere (minimal).
hamming.when: After patching gives you a candidate circuit, and before you believe it or build interventions on it.
hamming.why: Diagrams that fit the plots can still be wrong; these tests turn a story into a checkable claim, even when backup heads hide importance.

object.title: The crew board
object.subtitle: One row per crew member, one column per group sent home first; bar height is how much losing that member then hurts.

knobs.label: how fully h1 covers for h0

cap.1: Each row is one crew member; each column is a different group sent home first. Height: how much losing that member then hurts.
cap.2: Minimality scores |F(C∖(K∪v)) − F(C∖K)| for a toy circuit: rows are heads v, columns are knockout sets K.
cap.3: Toy F with a mover/backup pair (h0, h1), an inhibition multiplier (h2), a negative head (h3) and a small helper (h5).

cap.1: The first column: remove h0 alone and nothing happens, because h1 steps in. h0 looks like a spare part.
cap.2: With K empty, the mover and its backup each score zero: single-head ablation misses both.
cap.3: At K = ∅, redundancy masks both h0 and h1; this is why single ablations understate importance.

cap.1: Now send h1 home first: losing h0 suddenly hurts a lot. It was essential all along.
cap.2: At K = {h1}, h0's score jumps to 2. Minimality only asks for one K where the head matters.
cap.3: At K = {h1}, removing h0 drops F from 1.5 to −0.5, so h0 passes minimality.

cap.1: Switch the backup off: now h0 matters on its own, and h1 never matters at all. h1 is a spare part to cut.
cap.2: With no backup behaviour, h0 scores 2 even with K empty, and h1's row is flat, so h1 fails minimality.
cap.3: With backup = 0, h1's maximum over K is 0: remove it from C. Minimality prunes components with no effect in any context.

cap.1: From above: every row has a tall bar somewhere, so every member earns a place on this crew.
cap.2: A head's minimality is its tallest bar. All five pass here, with the helper h5 the smallest.
cap.3: Report each head's maximum over the tested K; a small maximum, like h5's 0.3, flags a weak member worth a second look.

predict.q: You ablate head 9.9 alone and the logit difference barely moves. Is 9.9 unimportant?

options.t: Not necessarily: a backup may be covering for it
Yes: drop it from the circuit

predict.why: Backup name movers take over when primary ones are ablated, so single-head ablation understates importance.

predict.q: Your circuit scores clearly higher than the full model. Is it faithful?

options.t: No: faithful means close to the model, not better

predict.why: A too-good circuit has probably left out heads that push against the answer, like the negative name movers.

predict.q: Which test catches a head that never matters in any situation?
predict.why: Minimality asks whether each head matters for some knockout set; a spare part matters for none.

object.where: Any claim that 'these parts do the job': circuits, ablation studies, minimal bug reproductions.
